transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-06-13
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes (approx)
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Ethan Clarke (Redwood SE), Lena Ortiz (Head of Infra - CopperGate), Tomás Rivera (Cloud Architect), Priya Shah (Security Lead)

Summary:
Quick intake to validate CopperGate's private deployment constraints: VPC peering vs private endpoints, egress IP allowlist, KMS/HSM requirements, regional gating. Confirm next steps for short bench test and send security artifacts.

Topics: VPC peering options, Private Link/private endpoints, transit gateway patterns, egress NATs, KMS integration, SOC2/SSO, latency targets for inference.

[00:00] Maya Patel: hey everyone, thanks for joining. do we have audio ok?
[00:08] Lena Ortiz: yep, good here. thanks for slotting us in, Maya.
[00:12] Maya Patel: awesome. quick intros? i am maya - account exec for redwood inference - and ethan is our solutions engineer.
[00:18] Ethan Clarke: hey all. i'll be the deep dive person on network and perf.
[00:22] Tomás Rivera: tomás, cloud architect on our infra team.
[00:25] Priya Shah: priya, security.

[00:30] Maya Patel: perfect. high level from you, lena - what are you trying to accomplish with redwood?
[00:38] Lena Ortiz: we're evaluating moving some of our model serving off our in-house cluster to either a hosted or private option. we like cost predictability so dedicated or private is interesting. main ask is network posture — we cannot have public endpoints, so private-only connectivity is required. also region lock to eu-west-1 for a portion of traffic.

[01:05] Maya Patel: makes sense. when you say private-only, do you mean peering between your VPC and redwood's VPC, or would you consider private endpoints (privatelink style)?
[01:12] Tomás Rivera: both are possible, but our security folks prefer private endpoints because it avoids transitive routing through our side — simpler auditing. however, peering could be easier for larger throughput.

[01:28] Priya Shah: yeah, we prefer minimal cross-account routing. plus we have strict egress allow-lists. we need fixed egress IPs for regulatory partners.

[01:36] Ethan Clarke: understood. to call out differences — peering gives L3 connectivity and generally lower latency, but then you need to manage route tables and potentially your transit gateway if using centralised network. private endpoints (redwood private endpoint) are interface endpoints — they terminate in our infra and give you a private IP to talk to. throughput and scaling patterns differ.

[01:58] Tomás Rivera: when you say "redwood private endpoint" — is that the hosted privatelink or the dedicated private fabric? we saw docs that mentioned Redwood Dedicated and Redwood Private and a 'privet' option in the quickstart (lol transcription glitch in doc).

[02:12] Maya Patel: yeah, apologies for the docs naming — sometimes the quick summary gets smushed. we have Hosted API (public), Dedicated (reserved capacity w/ dedicated GPU pool), and Private which is the VPC/on-prem deployment. the Private path supports private endpoints and peering depending on cloud provider. we'll send the diagram.

[02:32] Ethan Clarke: to add — we support interface endpoints in AWS Privatelink, and on peering we can accept cross-account peering connections. if you're using a transit gateway and central egress, we can peer to that TGW as well.

[02:48] Priya Shah: what about egress IPs? we need a small set of static IPs for allow-listing downstream apis. how do you handle egress when we peer?

[02:59] Ethan Clarke: couple options — egress from our side uses NAT IPs that are stable per-region for Private customers. for Dedicated, we can allocate specific egress IPs or use BYO-NAT patterns depending on contract. for peering, typically outbound to your services would come from your side, but calls originating in our infra to external services will use our egress pool unless tunneled.

[03:22] Lena Ortiz: hmm ok. can we route egress through our NAT? we want outbound egress logged and go through our proxies.

[03:28] Ethan Clarke: yes — if you peer and set route tables so our model servers reach external endpoints via your side, the traffic can NAT on your side. that's common in setups where customer wants control over egress and audit.

[03:40] Tomás Rivera: what's the latency penalty on privatelink vs peering? we have strict SLOs — inference tail latency must stay under 120ms 95pct for most use cases.

[03:52] Ethan Clarke: great question. rough ballpark we see: peering often gives the best latency because it's L3 direct, interface endpoints add some small overhead (10-30ms in some setups) due to proxying/ENI hops. but depends on AZ placement and cross-account path. for eu-west-1 local traffic peering should be fine. we'll run a bench test to measure real numbers.

[04:12] Priya Shah: and does redwood support pinning model versions? we need rollback and audit logs.

[04:17] Maya Patel: yes — you can pin model versions, control rollouts, and the console has traces and token-level cost/latency breakdowns. we also provide audit logs and can push them to a customer SIEM via syslog or S3.

[04:30] Tomás Rivera: any requirements for cross-account IAM roles or just peering+security groups?

[04:36] Ethan Clarke: for Privatelink we usually create service consumer endpoints in your account and service provider resources on our side; we might ask for a role to allow handshake for DNS entries but it's minimal. for peering it's mostly route tables, security groups, and the ASN for BGP if using edge-to-edge. no mandatory cross-account roles unless you want automated DNS validation.

[04:56] Lena Ortiz: we also need KMS integration — keys must be customer-managed and kept in our tenant. can Redwood integrate with our KMS/HSM for model artifacts and logs?

[05:05] Ethan Clarke: yes. we support customer-managed keys for encryption at rest. for Private deployments we can either integrate with your KMS over cross-account roles or you can escrow keys in an HSM if on-prem. there are some network and IAM steps for key policies.

[05:18] Priya Shah: is hardware HSM supported? we have a FIPS requirement for a subset of workloads.

[05:23] Ethan Clarke: we have HSM integrations for Private customers; depends on deployment mode — on-prem bundle supports local HSM, VPC private can use cloud HSM with key policies set to your account. we'll include the KMS integration guide.

[05:34] Maya Patel: quick question on scale — what's your expected throughput and concurrency? helps figure peering vs endpoint sizing.

[05:40] Lena Ortiz: initially low — around 10 rps with bursts to 60 rps for batched jobs. tokens per request variable; these are big context runs sometimes but can be batched.

[05:50] Ethan Clarke: ok that looks doable on either path. if you anticipate high parallel small requests, peering + dedicated capacity might be more cost-effective. for bursty large token jobs private endpoints with autoscaling pools are fine too.

[06:05] Tomás Rivera: any country/regional gating? we need eu only for a subset — can we ensure nodes only in eu-west-1 and traffic never leaves region?

[06:14] Maya Patel: yes we support region pinning for Private deployments. we can limit inference placement to eu-west-1 and refuse cross-region fallback unless you enable it. that will be in the deployment config and SLA.

[06:26] Priya Shah: log retention and access controls — can we SSO into console? SAML?

[06:31] Maya Patel: yep SAML SSO is supported, RBAC roles, and audit logs. SOC2 and ISO docs will be in the pack i'll send.

[06:40] Tomás Rivera: on peering, any limitations on CIDR overlap? we use 10.0.0.0/12 across our infra.

[06:47] Ethan Clarke: we cannot peer if CIDRs overlap. common fixes: use NAT/proxy or pick a non-overlapping prefix for the peering segment. we also support private endpoint DNS which avoids routing conflicts.

[06:58] Lena Ortiz: ok. about the bench test — what do you need from us to run a private endpoint latency test?

[07:06] Ethan Clarke: ideally a small test harness: curl-style requests or a simple client inside your VPC hitting the private endpoint with a representative prompt. we'll need the peering req (if peering) or consumer endpoint ARN (if privatelink), sample payloads, and target SLOs. we can spin a temporary model variant that replicates your workload.

[07:26] Tomás Rivera: can we do encrypted data in transit using mutual TLS? we require mTLS for some partners.

[07:33] Maya Patel: yes, we support mTLS in private deployments, can exchange certs, and integrate with your CA. we'll include an mTLS checklist.

[07:43] Priya Shah: any gotchas we should be aware of? e.g., DNS resolution or cross-account ENI limits?

[07:49] Ethan Clarke: ENI limits can bite if you have many endpoints per AZ; we usually recommend consolidating endpoints or using peering for high count. DNS is usually handled by creating private hosted zones or linking via resolver rules; that part sometimes requires extra permissions.

[08:03] Lena Ortiz: good point. our infra team uses central resolver rules. will that play nice with privatelink?

[08:09] Ethan Clarke: yes, you can set resolver rules to forward to our resolver endpoint or vice versa; we have docs for both patterns.

[08:18] Maya Patel: i'll also call out the cost tradeoffs — privatelink endpoints have small per-GB data processing fees and ENI costs per AZ; peering is more straightforward but can increase operational overhead. we can model expected monthly cost based on your traffic.

[08:33] Tomás Rivera: do you have an example cost model?

[08:36] Maya Patel: i do — i'll attach a short spreadsheet. i'll share it after the call along with the SOC2 pack and our network diagram.

[08:44] Priya Shah: about legal/compliance — we will need DPA and a Data Processing Addendum that specifies EU data residency for the pinned region. is that supported?

[08:54] Maya Patel: yes, DPA with region restrictions is part of our enterprise agreements. we'll surface templates.

[09:02] Tomás Rivera: one more — CI/CD and deployment rollouts. if we pin model versions, can we do a canary rollout in the private environment?

[09:10] Ethan Clarke: yes — our rollout supports canary, A/B, automatic fallback to a previous model variant on error, and traffic split controls. that works with Private too, you just configure the routing policy.

[09:20] Lena Ortiz: great. any limitations on model size or quantized runtimes? we plan to serve gpt-ish open models that are large.

[09:28] Ethan Clarke: we support large models; for Private we can provision GPU instances accordingly. quantization is supported and we can recommend profiles to save cost. large KV cache sizes and sequence length will affect memory, so we'll dimension nodes accordingly.

[09:40] Priya Shah: do you run any background telemetry to our models? e.g., usage metrics or sample logs?

[09:47] Maya Patel: we collect operational metrics for performance and cost, but we don't surface customer content. audit logs and traces can be exported to your S3/SIEM if you'd like.

[09:58] Tomás Rivera: ok, i think we have enough to try a bench. schedule wise, next week looks good for us.

[10:05] Maya Patel: perfect. action items recap: i'll send SOC2/security pack, peering diagram, cost spreadsheet; ethan will draft a short bench plan; tomás will share VPC CIDR and proxy/egress details; lena/priya will confirm KMS and region gating constraints.

[10:24] Priya Shah: also expect questions from legal on DPA — we'll loop in procurement if we like the results.

[10:29] Maya Patel: understood. any other blockers?

[10:32] Lena Ortiz: none from infra. small note — some partners require IP ranges for allowlisting by Friday; so egress IPs would be helpful.

[10:40] Ethan Clarke: we'll prioritize grabbing the per-region egress IPs for Private customers and include them in the pack.

[10:46] Maya Patel: great. i'll put dates on the next steps in the calendar invite. thanks everyone.

[10:52] Tomás Rivera: thanks, bye.
[10:54] Maya Patel: bye.

Notes: references shared during call — network diagram (link: https://redwood.ai/docs/private-networking/diagram), SOC2 + KMS integration guide (link: https://redwood.ai/security/soc2), cost spreadsheet (internal link to drive).

End of transcript.
